Bullshit, but I'm assuming it's for reasons different from what /u/Tozetre said, thought they can be a factor. The origin of the problem is Amby Burfoot and his article at runner's world, and that apparently the people of life hacker just regurgitate what others write without understanding it.

Burfoot states that a 500 kcal deficit per day will produce a smaller effect over time due to metabolic adaptation; I agree with that statement, but that's why refeeds exist, additionally, as you lose weight your body needs less calories and that's why you're supposed to track progress and adjust the diet. What he should have written is that using the same meal and exercise plan over time will not provide the results you expect, and for that reason, you can choose a bigger deficit. This is all for the sake of simplicity, hoping that will help more people lose weight, even though readjusting a smaller deficit is a much better system than a static bigger deficit for the same points he raises in his article.

The problem starts with this:

According to Hall, in the first year of a new weight-loss program, most overweight people will lose about half the weight that the
3,500-calories rule predicts. In other words, over 12 months, the new rule is 7,000 calories = one pound.

It's not clear where Hall's (the guy from the National Institutes of Health) words end and where Burfoot's words begin, but I bet my left nut that Burfoot was the one that erroneously extrapolated, based on earlier writings in his article, that if people lose half the weight expected, that means 7,000 kcal equals one pound of fat. He even writes in the article that 3,500 kcal is what is required to 'burn' it in a lab.

TL;DR: lifehacker's Beth Skwarecki and runner's world Amby Burfoot are misinforming about the work of the National Institutes of Health.
